opus-5.5.text:
I think they're quite different, and both have been really valuable to me in different ways.

With my PhD advisor, the relationship was more of a mentorship. Especially early on, I was still learning how to do research at all: how to pick a problem, how to tell whether an idea is worth pursuing, how to write a paper that people actually want to read. My advisor gave me a lot of freedom, but also a lot of structure. They would push back when I was going down a rabbit hole, and they helped me develop taste. A lot of that guidance was implicit. You absorb how someone thinks just by working next to them for years.

With Abhishek, it feels much more like a partnership between peers. We come at problems from somewhat different angles, so a lot of the value comes from the friction between our perspectives. One of us will have an intuition, and the other will try to break it or formalize it. The conversations are faster and more informal. We might go back and forth on a whiteboard or a message thread for an hour and come out with something neither of us would have reached alone.

Another difference is responsibility. As a student, there's always someone more senior who is ultimately accountable for the direction. In a peer collaboration, you share that. Nobody is the safety net, so you have to be more honest about when something isn't working and more willing to say, "Let's drop this."

If I had to summarize: my advisor helped shape *how* I think about research, and working with Abhishek is where I get to test and stretch that thinking against someone who sees things differently. I'm grateful for both, and I don't think the second would work as well without the first.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they're almost opposite in texture, and I think I needed both.

With my PhD advisor, the relationship had a kind of vertical structure to it. He was the person who taught me how to ask a question properly, how to tell when a result was actually a result versus just something that happened to work on one benchmark. There was a lot of him pushing back on me, a lot of "why do you believe this?" and me going away for a week to find out whether I actually believed it. That's incredibly valuable, but it's also a relationship where you're being formed. You're learning taste from someone, and you're partly trying to earn their confidence.

With Abhishek it's much more horizontal. We came at things from different angles, so neither of us is really the senior one on any given problem. He'll have an intuition about why something should work at scale, and I'll have an intuition about why the data is lying to us, and we just argue it out in a doc or on a whiteboard until one of us concedes or we realize we're both half right. There's much less ceremony. If I have a half-baked idea at eleven at night, I'll just send it to him, and he'll either tear it apart in ten minutes or say "wait, actually," and then we're off.

The other difference is speed. In a PhD, the unit of work is kind of the paper, and papers take months. With Abhishek the unit of work is more like the experiment, or even the hypothesis. We'll kill an idea in two days if it's not going anywhere, and nobody's ego is attached to it.

But I'd say the thing my advisor gave me is what makes the collaboration with Abhishek actually productive. If I hadn't been trained to be skeptical of my own results, that fast, informal style would just produce a lot of confident nonsense. So one taught me rigor, and the other is where I get to use it at full speed.
